title: Proper Scoring Rules Are Not Interchangeable as Training Objectives
hook: Five scoring rules that all reward honest probabilities in theory produced five differently-behaved forecasters in practice — same accuracy, different shape of error.
key_points: Compares five proper scoring rules as reward functions for training LLM forecasters on binary questions about resolved real-world events.
All five share the same theoretical incentive to report probabilities truthfully, yet the resulting models differ in calibration and probability use.
The Brier-trained model had the lowest observed Brier score and highest AUC-ROC; the log-trained model the best log score and lowest calibration error.
Differences in aggregate accuracy and discrimination were smaller than differences in the bias/information/noise decomposition.
Takeaway: reward choice shapes not only how well a model forecasts but how its errors are structured.
Caveat the authors flag: each condition used a single seed, so some differences may be training stochasticity.
content_html: A proper scoring rule rewards a forecaster for reporting their honest probability. Several rules share that property, so it is tempting to treat them as interchangeable when picking a training objective. Turtel and colleagues — with Philip Tetlock among the authors — trained LLM forecasters on five proper scoring rules over binary questions about resolved real-world events, and found the resulting models are not the same model.
extra_html:
What differed

Aggregate accuracy and discrimination moved relatively little. Calibration, probability use, and the estimated split of error into bias, information, and noise moved a lot. The Brier-trained model had the lowest observed Brier score and highest AUC-ROC; the log-trained model had the highest observed log score and the lowest calibration error. Models with similar headline performance got there through different error structures.

The caveat

Each condition used a single seed, which the authors note means some differences may reflect training stochasticity. Taken with that caution, the finding is a useful reminder that a reward function's theoretical incentive does not determine the behavior it produces — you get the errors your objective shapes. Full comparison in the paper.

related.title: Hindcast: Replaying Prediction Markets to Evaluate LLM Forecasters
related.hook: Backtesting an LLM forecaster on past events mostly measures its memory, not its foresight — because it can retrieve after-the-fact reports or was simply trained on data closer to the event.

related.title: LLM Judges Can't Separate Trust from Truth
related.hook: Ask a judge model for a trust score and a correctness verdict and you get two numbers — but they're not two pieces of evidence. Change the source label and both move.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean for a scoring rule to be 'proper'?
flashcards.back_html: It gives the forecaster a theoretical incentive to report their true probability — any other report scores worse in expectation.

flashcards.prompt: What surprised the authors about training on five different proper scoring rules?

choices.text: Despite sharing the same truthfulness incentive, the trained models differed in calibration and error structure
Only one of the five rules produced a model that beat random guessing
Aggregate accuracy varied far more than calibration did

flashcards.explanation_html: Properness is a property of the incentive, not a guarantee that two rules shape a trained model the same way.

flashcards.prompt: Which caveat do the authors attach to their comparisons?
flashcards.back_html: Each training condition used a single seed, so some of the observed differences may reflect training stochasticity rather than the scoring rule.
